meta.title: Who really said "Keep your friends close, and your enemies closer"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Sun Tzu. The line is Michael Corleone's in The Godfather Part II (1974), written by Mario Puzo and Francis Ford Coppola. It's absent from The Art of War.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Keep your friends close, and your enemies closer'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Sun Tzu — it's a 1974 movie line. Michael Corleone says it in The Godfather Part II. No source predating the film has ever been found.

answer.label: Not Sun Tzu — actually Mario Puzo and Francis Ford Coppola
answer.authorName: Mario Puzo and Francis Ford Coppola
answer.authorDates: Puzo 1920–1999 · Coppola b. 1939 · co-wrote the screenplay of The Godfather Part II (1974)
answer.sourceLine: The line is film dialogue, not ancient strategy: Michael Corleone says it in The Godfather Part II (1974), from a screenplay by Mario Puzo and Francis Ford Coppola. Wikiquote files it under Sun Tzu’s misattributed quotes ↗ and reports that no published source has been found that predates the film ↗ — and a full-text search of the standard 1910 translation of The Art of War turns up nothing resembling it.

source.heading: The Godfather Part II (1974)

docMeta.dd: Mario Puzo and Francis Ford Coppola

source.excerpt: My father taught me many things here. He taught me in this room. He taught me: keep your friends close but your enemies closer.
trail: Wikiquote’s Sun Tzu page ↗ lists the quote in its Misattributed section, stating it “has often been attributed to Sun Tzu and sometimes to Petrarch” and that it “comes most directly from a line spoken by Michael Corleone in The Godfather Part II (1974), written by Mario Puzo and Francis Ford Coppola.”

Wikiquote’s page for the film ↗ carries the full scene and an editorial note that the line “has often been attributed to Sun Tzu and sometimes to Niccolò Machiavelli, but there are no published sources yet found which predate its use in this film.”

We searched the complete text of Lionel Giles’s 1910 translation of The Art of War at Project Gutenberg ↗: zero occurrences of “friends close” and zero of “enemies closer”. The nearest genuine line, at Chapter III, is “If you know the enemy and know yourself, you need not fear the result of a hundred battles” — a different claim.
The American Film Institute’s 100 Movie Quotes list ↗ ranks “Keep your friends close, but your enemies closer” at #58, crediting Michael Corleone, played by Al Pacino, in The Godfather Part II.
source.excerptNote: Michael is answering Frank Pentangeli, who wants to strike back at Hyman Roth. Michael’s point is tactical: appear to side with Roth’s allies, keep Roth relaxed and confident in the friendship, and use that access to find the traitor inside his own family. Note that he presents the maxim as something his father taught him — invented Corleone family lore, not a citation of any real strategist.

source.rightsHolder: Paramount Pictures (screenplay by Mario Puzo and Francis Ford Coppola)
source.rightsNote: The wording originates in the screenplay of The Godfather Part II, first released 12 December 1974 by Paramount Pictures ↗ — far later than 1931, so it is in copyright in the United States and is not a free-floating public-domain proverb. Sun Tzu’s ancient text is long out of copyright and Giles’s 1910 translation is public domain, but that is irrelevant here: this line is not in it.

author.name: Mario Puzo and Francis Ford Coppola
author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.metaLine: Puzo 1920–1999 · Coppola b. 1939 · screenwriters, The Godfather Part II (1974)
author.bio: Mario Puzo wrote the 1969 novel The Godfather and co-wrote the screenplays for Coppola’s first two Godfather films; Francis Ford Coppola directed them and shared the writing credit. The pair won the Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay for The Godfather Part II. Which of the two actually put this particular sentence on the page is not documented — the credit is joint, and neither has publicly claimed the line.

copyAttribution: "Keep your friends close, but your enemies closer." — Michael Corleone in The Godfather Part II (1974), screenplay by Mario Puzo and Francis Ford Coppola. Commonly misattributed to Sun Tzu; the line appears nowhere in The Art of War, and no source predating the film has been found.

misattribution.heading: Everyone who gets the credit, and why they shouldn't
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most reliably mis-sourced sentences in English. It gets pinned on whichever strategist the poster finds most impressive — and the real authors, two working screenwriters who are alive in living memory and won an Oscar for the script, almost never get named.

items.why: Wikiquote places the line in Sun Tzu’s Misattributed section ↗. Searching the full text of Lionel Giles’s 1910 translation of The Art of War ↗ returns no occurrence of “friends close” or “enemies closer”. His genuine, and different, line is about knowing an enemy, not staying near one.

Wikiquote notes Machiavelli “is also sometimes credited” and points to a genuinely different sentence in The Prince ↗ — that a prince finds it easier to make friends of men who were content under the former government. That is about co-opting former opponents after a takeover, not about keeping enemies close for surveillance.
Wikiquote records that the line is “sometimes” attributed to Petrarch ↗, without offering a source for it. No work of Petrarch’s has been produced to support the claim.

Even the popular phrasing is slightly off. Michael Corleone says “keep your friends close but your enemies closer,” and the American Film Institute lists it at #58 with “but” ↗. The “and” version that circulates online is a soft misquotation of a line people are already misattributing.

misattribution.truthLine: The line is 1974 film dialogue by Mario Puzo and Francis Ford Coppola. Wikiquote’s verdict is blunt: “there are no published sources yet found which predate its use in this film” ↗.

context.heading: Why a movie line became an ancient proverb
lead: The line works as strategy advice, and that is exactly why it drifted. A maxim that sounds like distilled statecraft invites a distinguished author, and Sun Tzu is the default signature for anything that sounds like distilled statecraft — which is how a 1974 mob movie ended up being quoted as a 2,500-year-old Chinese military classic.

The irony is that the film never claimed otherwise. Michael Corleone attributes it to his own father, in that room, as family lore — a piece of invented Corleone tradition. The attribution laundering happened afterward, in business books, LinkedIn posts and quote sites, as a fictional gangster’s inherited wisdom was quietly upgraded to the real thing.
context.detailsSummary: What Sun Tzu actually wrote about knowing your enemy
detailsBody: Sun Tzu does have a famous line about enemies, and it is genuinely his — but it is a different thought. In Lionel Giles’s 1910 translation, Chapter III closes: “If you know the enemy and know yourself, you need not fear the result of a hundred battles.” That is about knowledge, not proximity. It advises study, not a seat at your enemy’s table.

The Corleone line says something considerably more specific and more cynical: stay physically and socially close to the people who mean you harm, so you can watch them. Sun Tzu never recommends cultivating an enemy’s friendship as cover. Collapsing the two is how the misattribution survives casual fact-checking — the vibe matches, the text does not.
context.pull: Michael credits his father. The internet credits Sun Tzu. The credit belongs to two screenwriters.
